process: D20: two blind graders (D7), adjudicator on disagreements, agent audit of agreed verdicts (D11)

verdicts.reason: Both graders agree on the fact: Google Translate's Android Conversation Mode launched January 2011 (English-Spanish; 14 languages by October 2011). D16 grades hit if true by target_year + 2; January 2011 is well inside the 2010+2 window, and the rule does not penalise arrival within two years. Grader B applied a late-arrival penalty that D16 does not impose inside the +2 window. Hit.

The sentence follows the body-LAN sentence and says 'these truly personal computers', so the referent is the small carried devices, not notebooks. In 2009 phones and smartphones used flash memory only, and most music players were flash (nano, shuffle, touch). This meets the device test (more than 50% of new units). Notebooks still used hard disks, but the text does not refer to them. Grader B's notebook reading is less faithful to the antecedent.

Grader B says no such device existed by 2009. That is wrong. Benenson and Shapiro demonstrated a programmable autonomous molecular computer in 2001 and in 2004 an autonomous DNA automaton that evaluated cancer-gene expression and on its own released an antisense drug molecule. Autonomous DNA walkers were shown in 2003-2004. Nanoengineering was not a practical technology in 2009. Both halves hold. The devices are molecular, not Drexler-style atom-by-atom assemblers; the text's 'molecule by molecule' covers them.

Routine-use test: more than 20% of the relevant industry. In 2009, 94% of US public school teachers used grading systems, 96% word processing and 94% the internet for instruction or administration; 97% of schools had classroom computers. 'All facets' is an overstatement, but routine use far above the 20% threshold across teaching and administration meets the rule. B's 'computer-centred instruction' test adds a condition the text does not state.

Both trends were real by 2009. World printing and writing paper production peaked in 2007 at about 120 Mt and fell in 2008-2009, and has not regained the peak. Google had scanned about 7 million books by November 2008 and 12 million by June 2010. Grader A tested completion (share of all titles scanned), but the text claims a rate, not completion.

In 2009 the share was near zero, so no hit and no 'measurable by 2009' partial. The question is the 3-5 year window. Sub-pound high-resolution tablets arrived in 2012-2013 (iPad mini 0.68 lb, Nexus 7, Kindle Fire HD). Pearson's 2013 survey found about three in ten US students in grades 4-12 owned a tablet, with younger students more likely; 42% of high-school students used tablets regularly in 2014. A large part of the tablets children owned were 7-8 inch models under a pound. This puts ownership of a matching device near the 20% line in 2013-2014. Grader A's claim of under 5% by 2014 is not supported. Low certainty: no source splits student tablet ownership by weight.

The text says materials 'are accessed through wireless communication'; it does not say 'mainly'. Routine-use test (20% of the relevant industry): in fall 2008, 39% of US public schools had whole-school wireless and 30% partial wireless, 58% had laptop carts, and 94% of teachers used the internet for instruction or administration. Wireless access to learning materials was routine in well over 20% of schools. B's 'mainly wireless' test adds a word the text does not contain.

The claim has three parts. Part 1 (teacher-led instruction still prevalent) is true. Part 2 (increasing reliance on software approaches) has a measurable share: 55% of US school districts had students in distance-education courses in 2009-10, with about 1.8 million enrollments, and cognitive tutors ran in thousands of schools. Part 3 (teachers attend primarily to motivation and well-being) did not happen by 2014. A measurable share above 5% but below mainstream by 2009 fits partial. A's miss grades only part 3.

Acceptance is measurable where the systems were used. Print-to-speech software (Kurzweil 3000 and similar) was used and accepted among students with learning disabilities. The LeapFrog Tag, a pen that reads printed children's books aloud, sold more than 2 million readers in 2008-2009, a share above 5% of US children of the target age. General routine use by most children (claim 040) did not happen. Measurable, below mainstream, gives partial. A's miss rests on 'under 5%' without a source and ignores consumer read-aloud devices.

The only measured quantity is formal learning time: about 32 hours per employee per year around 2009-2011, about 1.6% of a 2,000-hour year, and flat, not growing. No source shows learning as a significant share of work time in most jobs, by 2009 or by 2014. B's test (share of workers who get some training) measures a different claim (see 047). Informal learning is not measured, so it cannot support a hit or partial.

Routine-use test (20% of the relevant population). In 2004-05, 27% of US adults took work-related courses in one year, the most common adult-education activity. Employers delivered about 32 formal learning hours per employee every year, and many licensed professions required continuing education. Recurring training reached well over 20% of workers. 'Most careers' is not directly measured, but the rule's mainstream threshold is met.

The verb is 'have been introduced'. Talking GPS devices for blind travellers were on sale: Trekker (reviewed 2003), BrailleNote GPS, and Trekker Breeze ($895, reviewed March 2009), which announced streets and intersections and guided users back to route. In the sentence, GPS attaches most naturally to 'finding their way around'; separate electronic obstacle aids also existed. GPS did not detect obstacles, which is a weakness in wording, not a failure of the main claim.

No real-time speech translation was in common use in 2009, so the share was under 5% at the placed year. Google Translate added speech input in 2010 and an experimental English-Spanish conversation mode in January 2011; use stayed far below 20% through 2014. Neither partial condition holds: no 5% share by 2009, and no mainstream use in 2012-2014. B's partial rests on 'likely above 5% of smartphone users trying it', which is not a D16 condition.

User test (20% of target users in major markets). By April 2009, 56% of US adults had gone online wirelessly (Wi-Fi or mobile), and Kindle and iPhone delivered books, music and apps over the air. A used mobile broadband subscriptions worldwide (13%), which excludes Wi-Fi and averages in non-major markets. 'Ever-present, high-bandwidth' overstates 2009 coverage, but wireless delivery was mainstream in major markets.

The book itself places this as a non-mainstream practice, so the mainstream test does not apply; the test is presence at a measurable level. Remote sexual activity was practised in 2009: webcam sex, cybersex, and avatar sex in Second Life adult regions (peak 88,200 concurrent users in 2009). In 2012, 6% of US adult cell owners had sent and 15% had received a sext. A's VR-mainstream reading contradicts the author's own next sentence.

Popular means mainstream here. No source shows virtual-partner use at 5% or more of adults in major markets by 2009 or by 2014. LovePlus (Japan only, September 2009) and adult areas of Second Life were niches. Both graders agree use was niche; B gives partial without a 5% figure, and D16 partial needs a measurable share of at least 5%.

The observable part has a dominant reading and data: a 2007 Duke/Berkeley study found a foreign-born key founder in 25.3% of US engineering and technology companies founded 1995-2005, with $52bn in 2005 sales. The 'ideal heritage' explanation is opinion and cannot be tested, but an untestable explanation does not give a different verdict; no faithful reading of the text gives a miss. D16 allows unfalsifiable only when readings give different verdicts.

Mixed. OECD 2009 data name Israel, Sweden, Switzerland, the UK and the US as the developed venture-capital markets; Japan is not among them and only 2% of Japanese start-ups got VC, so Europe ahead of Japan holds. Korea is a counterexample: OECD ranks it among the leading countries in VC as a share of GDP. Venture capital stayed under 0.05% of GDP in most countries in 2009, so 'popular throughout the world' is only partly true, though VC and employee share schemes existed in many countries. One comparison holds, one fails: partial.

Mainstream test (20% of target users). By 2009 the iTunes Store was the largest US music vendor (from April 2008), had previews and secure checkout, and was on iPhone over Wi-Fi and 3G from 2007; the App Store passed 1 billion downloads in April 2009. Download over home Wi-Fi to laptops was common (56% of US adults online wirelessly in 2009). A's own test, 35% smartphone ownership in May 2011, is within 2 years and above 20%, which D16 grades as a hit.

Computerworld (28 Aug 2000) gives about 60 embedded processors per US household, and Turley (2002, found by search) gives 40-50; no source measures the 2009 figure. Both graders chose partial without an actual value, so the D16 quantitative band cannot be applied.

The sentence depends on claim 101 (a growing neo-Luddite movement), which did not appear in measurable form. The predicate 'influence is limited' is true; the presupposed movement and the causal mechanism fail or cannot be tested. Neither reading is more faithful to the text: the sentence asserts the limit and presupposes the movement equally. The readings give hit and miss. D16 gives unfalsifiable.

FRED/Census SAIPE confirms poverty 11.9% (1999) and 14.3% (2009); a 'stable' forecast of 11.9% is 16.8% off the actual 14.3%, and the count (32.8M vs 43.6M) is 24.8% off, so both measures fall inside the D16 25% band. Grader B's statement that both exceed 25% is an arithmetic error; 'continuing concern' held.

The observable state held: the poor did not form a significant political movement in 2009-2011, and public assistance expanded (ARRA raised SNAP benefits from April 2009; participation peaked at 47.6 million in 2013). The 2009 recession raised poverty to 14.3%, but US income per head stayed among the highest in the world, so 'generally high level of affluence' is weakened, not false. Occupy (2011) was not an underclass movement. The mechanism cannot be tested, but no faithful reading gives a miss on the observable state. Low-to-medium certainty.

Auto-accompaniment was in wide amateur use: arranger keyboards follow the chords a player enters live and generate a backing band, and Band-in-a-Box (since 1990) generates backing and solos. That is a basic 'cybernetic musician' that responds to the player's chords, and its use by amateur keyboard players is a measurable share. Responsive improvising partners stayed in research labs, so 'routinely jam' with responsive musicians was not mainstream by 2014. Measurable but below mainstream gives partial. No usage statistics exist, so certainty is low.

The software existed by 2009: Band-in-a-Box, GarageBand with Magic GarageBand (bundled with every Mac), and Microsoft Songsmith (early 2009), which generates accompaniment for a sung melody. Under D16 the claim reads as mainstream use, and no source shows 20% of non-musician music lovers creating music with such software by 2011. Products on sale and bundled at scale, with thousands of shared user songs, show measurable use below mainstream. B's availability reading ignores the D16 frame.

Machine translation was in mass use by 2009-2011: Google Translate (2006; about 23 languages by January 2009), Babel Fish, Bing Translator and Chrome's built-in page translation (2010). Google Translate served over 200 million people a day by May 2013. Casual use by internet users reading foreign-language text meets the mainstream test. B's narrower reading (publication-grade translation of books) adds a restriction the text does not state. Medium certainty: no retrieved figure for 2009-2011 exactly.

In the book's 2009 chapter, virtual environments are screen and eyeglass based (claims 010, 017, 073); immersive direct-eye VR is placed in the 2019 chapter. So the dominant 2009 reading is interactive environments as software, which covers games and simulations. In 2008, 53% of US adults and 97% of teens played video games, and World of Warcraft had over 10 million subscribers. That clears the 20% mainstream test. The rafting and movie-star examples are illustrative; the movie-star example did not occur.

The sentence is mainly a statement of limit, and the limit held: consumer haptics in 2009 were controller rumble and force-feedback wheels and joysticks. The audiovisual part holds under the same reading as claim 123: 3D game environments with surround sound were a mass entertainment form in 2009. A graded 'compelling VR' as consumer head-mounted VR, which the book places in 2019, not 2009.

Wikipedia confirms Cyber Command was ordered 23 Jun 2009 as a sub-unified command and elevated only in 2017; GAO-11-695R puts DoD cybersecurity budget estimates at $2.3-3.2B for FY2012, under 1% of the DoD budget. The claimed 'primary focus' did not occur by 2014, and no D16 branch gives partial.

Dominance was not reached: in 2009 the wars were fought mainly by about 186,000 US ground troops and manned aircraft, and drones were remotely piloted, not autonomous. But unmanned aircraft had a large measurable share: DoD inventory grew from 167 in 2002 to nearly 7,500 in 2010, and the unmanned share of DoD aircraft rose from 5% in 2005 to about 41% by 2010-2012. A measurable share well above 5% but short of dominance by the placed year gives partial.

Computerised records were mainstream among office physicians by 2011 (57% any EMR, 34% basic), so the loose reading is a hit. But the text says lifetime records. Longitudinal lifetime records existed only in integrated systems (VA, Kaiser) and some small national systems; records elsewhere stayed fragmented across providers through 2014. A measurable share (more than 5% of US patients in VA and Kaiser alone is near the line) below mainstream gives partial. B's reading drops the word that makes the claim a forecast.

Attention rose around 2008-2009. Springer published 'Parsing the Turing Test' (January 2008), a 518-page multi-author volume with a Dennett foreword. The 2008 Loebner Prize at the University of Reading, where programs fooled 3 of 12 judges, drew wide press coverage. The 2012 centenary was larger, but 'renewed interest' needs a visible rise, not a peak, and the rise is dated 2008. Medium certainty: no attention index was retrieved.

The first clause (computers still fail) is true. The forecast is the trend in confidence, and the text does not say whose. The only survey (AGI-09, self-selected optimists) supports reading 1; mainstream AI opinion of the period was more sceptical, and the 2002 Kapor-Kurzweil bet framed the question as open. No series measures a change in confidence between 1999 and 2009. Neither reading dominates, the readings point to different verdicts, and the trend itself has no measure.

Compound claim. The communication half held strongly (93% of world population within 3G+ reach, 95% mobile-broadband coverage by 2021; 4G speeds orders above 1999 dial-up). The 'computing embedded everywhere' half (ubiquitous computing in objects) was only partly realised by 2021 (see the separate 148 claim). One half mainstream, one half below it = partly true. Partial.

Grader A called it ungradable for want of a direct workload-share series, but the claim is a 'majority' (>50%) threshold that bounding evidence clearly falsifies: in 2019-2024 the overwhelming bulk of executed compute ran conventional software (OS, web, databases, business apps), AI-accelerated servers were a minority even of data-centre growth, and genetic algorithms are marginal. A threshold this far from met does not need a precise series to be graded, so D22 ungradable does not apply. Miss.

The sentence predicts two modes: reading on hand-held screens and, as the more common mode, direct-eye displays. Hand-held reading became routine and mainstream (phones, tablets, e-readers carried the majority of reading). The 'more commonly direct-eye' mode failed (AR/retinal eyewear stayed niche). One named mode held at mainstream, the dominant mode failed = partly true. Grader A graded only the failed direct-eye mode; the hand-held clause is part of the forecast and held. Partial.

The claim's wording is 'very effective and widely used', not 'used by a majority of candidates'. Both parts held: implants are the established, highly effective standard of care for severe-to-profound deafness, with ~736,900 registered worldwide by December 2019 (over 1 million by 2022) and routine deployment across all major markets, including the majority of eligible children in developed countries. Grader B's 20%-of-all-candidates test reads in a penetration threshold the claim does not state. Hit.

The verb is 'have emerged' - an existence/appearance claim, not a mainstream-adoption claim. Commercial glasses-free 'holographic' light-field displays existed by 2018 (Looking Glass shipped December 2018), satisfying emergence. Grader B graded down because true diffraction holograms remained prototypes, but that imposes a stricter definition than the label's 'emerged'. The dominant reading of the claim is met. Hit.

Under the decade-chapter rule (hit if true by target_year + 2 = 2021), the claim held: by 2020-2021 meetings moved online at scale (Zoom to >300 million daily participants April 2020; 67% of US white-collar workers remote in part by September 2021), so most meetings did not require physical proximity. The rule grades the outcome inside the window; the pandemic cause and the later partial reversal do not disqualify a within-window hit. Grader A's requirement of a durable majority of all meetings is stricter than D16's window test. Hit.

Two components. The 'all done through the ever-present web' component held near-universally (streaming, web-delivered media and calls were ubiquitous by 2019). The 'via worn/direct-eye devices' delivery mechanism failed (media ran on phones/PCs/TVs; AR/VR headsets 11.2M shipments in 2021, far below any share threshold; 3D calls niche). One component true at mainstream, the specific delivery mechanism below 5% = partly true. Grader A graded only the worn-device mechanism; the web-delivery of these activities is real and massive. Partial.

The claim is modest ('superior in SOME ways, such as...') and names two specific advantages: very reliable memory and programmable personalities. Both held by 2019-2021: assistants and companion apps (Replika, voice assistants used by ~1 billion people) had exact recall of stored data and configurable, scripted personas. Grader A graded down on conversational-memory limits, but the claim's 'very reliable memories' points to stored-data recall, which digital systems trivially have. The stated narrow superiorities held. Hit.

First clause held throughout 2019-2021 (chatbots widely seen as far less subtle than humans). The second clause only requires that 'there is disagreement', a low bar met by 2019-2021: companion-app users (Replika) treated bots as partners, a visible minority dissent, later sharpened by the June 2022 LaMDA episode. Grader A set the bar at a prominent public controversy and so dated it to 2022; the claim's wording ('there is disagreement') was already satisfied within the 2019+2 window. Hit.

The dominant reading of 'sufficient prosperity to provide' is a capacity claim, not a claim that necessities are universally provided, so this is not a case of two equally faithful readings diverging - D16 unfalsifiable does not apply, and Grader B's call is set aside. Under the dominant (capacity) reading: the controversies-persist clause held (welfare/responsibility debates continued), and aggregate world output could cover basic necessities at modest cost; but necessities were in fact not secured for ~700 million people in extreme poverty, so the implied state of affairs was only partly realised. Partly true. Partial.

The claim states a specific quantity: the share of working time (across most jobs) spent on the employee's own learning, and that it is growing. No public series measures this. Grader A graded partial off adult-learning participation rates (share of adults who take any training), which is a different quantity - a proxy, not a measure of the stated share of work time. Under D23 a proxy of another quantity is not a measure. Ungradable (looked for: share of working time spent learning across employment; ATD State-of-the-Industry hours-per-employee and OECD/Eurostat adult-learning participation measure neither the share of work time nor its trend).

By 2018-2019 AI artists were emerging and taken seriously in visual art (Edmond de Belamy sold at Christie's for $432,500, 2018) and music (AIVA recognised by SACEM, 2016), but critics largely treated these as novelty, and 'all of the arts' (literature and others) lagged. Wide serious engagement across the arts arrived with the 2022-2024 generative-AI wave (within the 3-5-year window). The claim's qualifiers ('all', 'taken seriously') were only partly met by 2021. Grader A's hit undervalues those qualifiers. Partial.

Cited sources (Wikipedia 'Midjourney', 'Theatre D'opera Spatial', 'AIVA') are anecdotes with no share of working artists using AI, in 2019 or 2022-2024, so neither the >=5% nor the mainstream-in-3-5-years branch is shown. Readings also split: machine-intelligence features in standard tools (auto-tune, content-aware fill) were typical in 2019, which would read as hit.

Video games clearly surpassed film and recorded music by revenue (US games matched US film at ~$43bn in 2018; global games ~$179bn 2020, ~$191bn 2021, roughly double film). But the claim is 'the type ... in greatest demand ... continues to be', i.e. the single largest over all entertainment, and television/video (pay-TV plus advertising plus streaming) remains a larger aggregate that neither grader shows smaller. Games is the largest discrete interactive product but not clearly the single greatest entertainment product overall. Partly true. Partial.

World Bank SP.DYN.LE00.IN 2019 vs 100 years (D16 numeric, error relative to actual): World 72.9 (37%, miss), US 78.8 (27%, miss), but EU 81.3 (23%), OECD 80.2 (24.6%), high income 80.2 (24.7%) and Japan 84.4 (18.5%) are within 25%, i.e. partial. The industrial-revolution frame points to developed countries, which sit at the partial/miss boundary; A misapplied the band (miss at 15%) and B wrongly said the developed-country reading is a miss.

The 2017 horsepox synthesis (~$100,000, mail-order DNA, a funded university team) shows the capability had descended to a modestly resourced lab and drew expert alarm - but it required ~$100k, specialised tacit skill and controls, which is above the claim's specific 'typical graduate student' threshold. Grader A equates 'academic lab/team' with 'typical graduate student'; the claim names the latter. Capability trending toward but not yet at the stated level = partly true. Partial.

The claim has checkable components, so D22 ungradable (Grader B) does not apply. The 'major focus of international security agencies' component is falsifiable and largely failed pre-COVID (the 2018 US National Defense Strategy centred on great-power competition, not biothreats); bioengineered countermeasures did advance (mRNA design in days; first authorisation Dec 2020) but were not recognised as a 'comparable' offset and biosecurity was not the agencies' major focus in 2019. Part true, part false. Partial.

The 'do not meet expert criteria' clause held strongly (Eugene Goostman's 2014 'pass' widely rejected by experts). But the 'prevalent reports' clause was not met by 2019: Turing-pass reports were occasional (Goostman and a few chatbot claims), not prevalent, until the generative-AI wave of 2022-2023, 3-4 years after target (within the 3-5-year window). Grader A's hit understates 'prevalent'. Partly true. Partial.

The consensus clause ('not yet passed') held firmly through 2019-2021. The 'growing controversy' clause, read as a genuine live dispute over whether machines had passed a valid test, materialised with large language models in 2022-2024 (LaMDA sentience claim June 2022; 'ChatGPT broke the Turing test' 2023; GPT-4/GPT-4.5 pass studies 2024-2025), 3-5 years after target. In 2019-2021 the matter was relatively settled among experts. Partly true (consensus held; the growing controversy came in the 3-5-year window). Partial.

The dominant reading - devices tapping vast remote compute and memory over high-speed links - was realised by 2010-2012 via cloud computing (AWS 2006, Azure 2010) plus mobile broadband, with mobile apps routinely offloading to the cloud. The parenthetical 'mesh' (every device becoming a web server in a peer supercomputer) is Kurzweil's gloss on the architecture and did not form, but the substantive claim held. Grader B weights the failed peer-mesh detail over the realised substance. Hit.

Always-on wireless Internet was arriving (3G smartphones gave constant connectivity, LTE launched Dec 2009), satisfying 'at all times'. But 'very high-bandwidth' is the load-bearing qualifier: around 2010-2012 most mobile data still ran on 3G (a few Mbps), and very-high-bandwidth 4G/LTE did not reach mainstream (~20% of users in major markets) until ~2013-2014 - mainstream 3-5 years after the placed year. Grader A counts the LTE launch but it was not widespread by 2012. Partly true. Partial.

Read in context (items 004-007 describe tiny displays projecting images, AR overlays and augmented perception), 'project auditory environments' means immersive/spatial soundscapes, not ordinary stereo earphones. Immersive spatial audio in tiny earbuds arrived ~2020 (AirPods Pro spatial audio), ten years late and beyond the 5-year window. The trivial 'personal audio' reading that Grader B uses treats the prediction as the already-mundane earphone, which is not the dominant contextual reading. Miss.

Around 2010 AR existed only as niche smartphone apps (Layar/Wikitude 2009, Word Lens Dec 2010), well below the D16 5% partial floor, and mass AR use (Pokemon Go) did not arrive until July 2016 - six years later, outside the 3-5-year mainstream window. Neither D16 partial condition is met (no >=5% share by 2010-2012; mainstream not reached within 3-5 years). Grader B granted partial on the mere existence of AR apps without a 5% share. Miss.

The claim's mechanism is brain scanning contributing to the model. By 2025-2026 it has not: the effective AI systems of the period (LLMs/GPT-4) are trained on text, not derived from brain scans, and connectomics remains at fruit-fly / ~1 mm3-mouse scale with no scan-derived model of human intelligence. Grader A graded partial by crediting LLMs, but LLMs do not satisfy 'brain scanning contributes'. The stated route did not deliver; a reversal by 2027-2030 is not supported by current connectomics. Miss (window nominally open to 2030, but the brain-scanning mechanism shows no sign of delivering).
